post.summary: Preview what an archive import would do, without changing anything
post.description:
Takes the same archive and the same flags as `workspace/{workspace_id}/import` and reports what that import WOULD do. It writes NOTHING: no object is created, updated or deleted, no table is dropped or truncated, and no row is loaded. Run this before a destructive import and confirm against its output. `operations[]` lists every object the import would `create`, `update` or `delete` and every table it would `truncate`; `summary` carries the same information as per-action and per-type counts, plus `summary.rows`, which reports the ROWS at stake — the tables that would be emptied by `truncate`, and the tables whose rows would be destroyed along with the table itself. The most important line to read is the one about a dropped table: `delete=true` deletes tables the archive does not carry, and every row in them goes too. `records=false` does not protect those rows, because it governs only the tables the archive carries. `has_records` is true only when the flags say rows would be loaded AND the archive actually carries them, so an archive exported without records never previews as writing rows. Combinations the import would refuse (`delete`, `records` or `truncate` with `mode=replace`, a merge with no destination, an archive whose objects have no guids under `delete=true`) are refused here too, with the same error. `preserve_guids` means here exactly what it means on the import route, and is accepted for one reason: with `mode=replace` it subjects the archive to a guid validity check, so an archive carrying duplicate or malformed guids is REFUSED. Send the same value you intend to import with, or this preview reports a clean plan for a call that then fails. Omitting it previews the historical behaviour — every object created under a freshly minted guid, and no such refusal. The output has the same shape as the multidoc dry run, so one client can render both. If the file is encrypted, the correct `password` is required to decrypt.

post.summary: Import an archive into a workspace, replacing or merging its content
post.description:
`mode=replace` (the default) wipes the workspace's existing content and configuration, then imports the archive in its place. `mode=merge` leaves the workspace's content in place and upserts the archive's objects into it by guid, so re-importing the same archive updates the objects it created previously instead of duplicating them. `delete=true` (merge only) additionally DELETES every object in the workspace that the archive does not carry, making the import a full sync. This drops tables and their data. It is rejected with `mode=replace`, and rejected for an archive whose objects have no guids. `records` and `truncate` (merge only, both default false) control whether the import touches table ROWS, for the tables the archive carries. With `truncate=false records=false` those rows are left untouched, which is why an unflagged merge cannot alter live data. With `truncate=false records=true` the archive's rows are upserted over what is there. With `truncate=true records=false` each table is emptied. With `truncate=true records=true` each table is emptied and then holds exactly the archive's rows. They mean the same as the flags of those names on the multidoc import. Both are rejected with `mode=replace`, which has already dropped every table and reloads all of the archive's rows regardless. Note that `records=false` protects rows only in tables the archive CARRIES: `delete=true` deletes tables the archive does not carry, and their rows go with them. `preserve_guids=true` makes the import store the GUID each archive object carries, instead of minting a fresh one per object — so an object keeps the same identity across re-imports of the same archive, which is what lets a later `mode=merge` match it and what the xanots CLI writes back into local `.xs` files. It applies to `mode=replace` only; a merge already preserves the archive's guids, by matching rows on them. It defaults to `false` and OMITTING IT KEEPS THE HISTORICAL BEHAVIOUR: every object is created under a freshly minted guid, exactly as this route has always done. With it set, the archive is additionally rejected up front if two objects of one type share a guid or a guid is malformed — identities that cannot be told apart would otherwise resolve references silently and arbitrarily. If the file is encrypted, the correct `password` is required to decrypt.
